In effect since 2021

Projects of 10+ homes that need a zoning change, city land or city money must rent 10–20% of units below market, priced for households at 60% of area median income on average. The rest of the building pays for those units, so a higher requirement means more affordable homes in each building, but some buildings stop making financial sense and never get built. Dropping it builds more homes but none of them affordable, and ends the in-lieu fees that fund affordable housing and rent help.

Applies to new buildings of 10+ homes, using a middle estimate (assumption): no requirement means about 20% more of those buildings, 10% about 10% more, 30% about 5% fewer. Terner Center's Los Angeles model shows about twice that (398,800 vs. 289,000 homes with no requirement vs. LA's current rule). Studies of real cities mostly find little or no drop in total building (California, the Bay Area, LA and Orange counties, Baltimore–Washington), with 5–8% fewer homes in one California study; Portland's permits fell sharply after its 2017 rule, but that isn't a controlled study. Dropping it builds more homes but none affordable, and ends the in-lieu fees, which go half to building affordable homes and half to rent help.

Mayor Johnson's 2024 report had 107 fixes to Chicago's approval process; the city says 96 were underway or done by May 2025. Zoning changes averaged 116 days to approve in 2017 (Chicago Cityscape).
Assumption: 10% more projects get built and they arrive about 7 months sooner (20% of a roughly three-year approval and build). Research finds 20–25% fewer permits in slow-approval metros.

Would let some mid-size apartment buildings use one stairway instead of two, which makes 4–6 story buildings work on narrow Chicago lots. The Buildings and Fire departments oppose it on safety grounds.

Mostly stuck, 2026

Chicago already approved or planned about 31,600 homes in a handful of giant projects: The 78 (10,000), Bronzeville Lakefront at the old Michael Reese site (6,800), the 1901 Project around the United Center (about 5,000, though its zoning allows up to 9,463), Cabrini-Green (4,080), Foundry Park on the old Lincoln Yards site (up to 3,737) and the rest of North Union (2,007). Most are stuck waiting on roads, bridges, river walls or gap financing. Flip this on and the city pays to unstick them.

Assumption: half of those 31,624 planned homes get built by 2041 once the city funds the infrastructure. That half is about a sixth of the normal-mode goal and about 5% of hard mode's, so everyday zoning still does most of the work. The purple buildings on the map show each whole plan built out by 2041, phase by phase, inside its approved zoning area and at the heights its plan allows (Foundry Park 8 to 38 stories at first, later towers 250–450 ft; the 1901 Project up to 660 ft; North Union up to 695 ft; Bronzeville Lakefront up to 350 ft in phase one; Cabrini-Green mostly six-flats, townhomes and mid-rises). Exact building spots follow each project's published site plan.
City is selling lots now
The city owns more than 7,100 vacant lots, concentrated in Englewood, West Englewood, New City and North Lawndale, and sells some for $1 through its Missing Middle program.
Assumption: half of the lots get a 2-flat within 15 years.
Pilot: Missing Middle, 2025–26

On much of the South and West Sides, a new 2-flat costs more to build than it would sell for, so lots stay empty even where zoning already allows homes. Chicago's Missing Middle program sells city lots for $1 and covers up to $150,000 per home; its fourth round is 62 homes on 30 lots. There are also about 31,000 privately owned vacant parcels in the city (Cook County Assessor, 2025). This scales the idea up to them.

Assumption: at up to $150,000 per home, 15% of private vacant parcels get a 2-flat by 2041 (about 9,400 homes, roughly $1.4B in subsidy, or about $94M a year), and rezoned projects in soft-market neighborhoods (demand under 0.9×) are 50% more likely to get built. The map shows the two-flats it builds.
Reform idea
Alderpeople can effectively veto housing in their wards. A 2023 federal HUD investigation found the practice blocks affordable housing (HUD withdrew the finding in 2025).
Assumption: 15% more projects get built everywhere because fewer are blocked.
Minneapolis, 2020

The 2040 plan allowed 3 homes on any lot and 3–6 stories on transit corridors; the city ended parking minimums in 2021. From 2017 to 2022 Minneapolis grew its housing 12% (vs 4% in the rest of Minnesota) and rents rose 1% (vs 14%). 87% of new homes were in buildings of 20+ units; only 1% were 2–4-unit buildings.
Every lot with 1–4 homes gets 3-flat zoning, corridor lots get mid-rise, and the no-parking boost applies citywide.
Cambridge, MA, 2025

Cambridge now allows 4 stories by right on nearly every residential lot (6 with affordable units) and dropped lot-size and unit caps. Early: about 400 homes permitted so far in 2026, vs about 350 starts a year in 2023–25.
Every lot with 1–4 homes gets at least 6-flat zoning. Early results are thin, so treat this as a what-if.
Houston, 1998 & 2013

Houston cut its minimum lot size from 5,000 to 3,500 sq ft by right, and as little as 1,400 for some subdivisions. Nearly 80,000 homes have been built on small lots, and townhouses replacing single-family homes had a median assessed value of $340,000 vs $545,000 for other new houses.
Assumption: 20% more 3-flat and 6-flat projects on lots of 5,000+ sq ft, which can split into townhomes.
Buffalo 2017, Austin 2023

Chicago dropped parking mandates near transit; Buffalo, Minneapolis and Austin dropped them citywide. In Buffalo, mixed-use projects built 53% fewer parking spaces than the old rules required. Austin's median rent fell from $1,546 to $1,296 (2021–2026) amid record building.
Assumption: 10% more projects get built on lots outside transit areas, where mandates still apply.
Texas, 2025
Texas SB 840 lets apartments and mixed-use go up on commercially zoned land without a rezoning. A coalition report counts 1,250+ homes directly enabled in its first year.
Lots on Chicago's commercial corridors get at least 6-flat zoning.
Vancouver, 2017

Vancouver taxes homes left empty (now 3% of value). Declared vacant homes fell 67% from 2017 to 2024 and the tax has put $194M toward affordable housing. Chicago has about 60,000 homes the Census counts as 'other vacant'.
Assumption: 10% of Chicago's 'other vacant' homes return to use. Many are in poor shape, so it's deliberately modest.
Montgomery County, MD, 2021

Montgomery County's $100M revolving fund (the model for Chicago's Green Social Housing) has 1,100+ homes built or underway and targets 6,000 over 20 years, at least 30% affordable. Chicago's fund is $135M.
Adds $270M to Chicago's fund at Montgomery County's target pace: about 12,150 homes in 15 years, 30% affordable.
Chicago, 1970s–2010s

Since the 1970s, Chicago alderpeople have downzoned dozens of neighborhoods, usually at neighbors' request. From 1990 to 2010, downzoned North Side and downtown areas grew their housing 1.8% while similar areas that weren't downzoned grew 9.6%. Downzoned areas also lost rental homes and were associated with higher home values.
Assumption: a new round of downzoning cuts the homes Chicago builds anyway by 25%. Areas you rezone keep your zoning.
Chicago ended them, 2025

In July 2025 Chicago voted to end parking requirements near transit, about 74% of the city. Bringing them back means every new building has to carve out space for cars again. Garage parking adds about $1,700 a year, or 17% of rent, to a typical apartment; even renters without a car pay about $621 a year for it.
Assumption: 15% fewer rezoned projects get built (parking eats lot space and budget), and 10% fewer of the homes Chicago builds anyway. Turns off "No parking minimums anywhere."
Chicago, 606 & Pilsen, 2021

Since 2021 Chicago has charged a fee to demolish homes near the 606 trail and in Pilsen, to slow gentrification; since 2024 it's $20,000 per home lost or $60,000 per building. Demolitions there fell 88% and 25% in the first year. It keeps the old buildings, but every one kept is a bigger building that doesn't go up. Research finds metros with slow approvals get 20–25% fewer permits.
Assumption: 20% fewer rezoned projects get built and they arrive 25% later (some slip past 2041), and 15% fewer of the homes Chicago builds anyway.
Rent control, including new buildings
Banned in Illinois since 1997

Illinois has barred cities from capping rents since 1997, and bills to lift the ban keep coming back. Rent control does help people who already have a home: in San Francisco, covered tenants were nearly 20% more likely to stay put. But landlords covered by the law cut their rental supply 15%, which pushed citywide rents up 5.1%. St. Paul capped rents at 3% in 2021, new buildings included; permits fell from over 2,000 a year to about 1,200 in 2022–23. The city has since exempted all new construction.

Assumption: 40% fewer rezoned projects of 3+ homes get built (about St. Paul's first-year drop), and 30% fewer of the homes Chicago builds anyway. The simulation doesn't count the real benefit to tenants who stay.
Los Angeles, 2023

LA's Measure ULA taxes property sales above about $5M at 4% and above $10M at 5.5%, to pay for housing. Big sales fell by about half. UCLA researchers first estimated 18% fewer apartments in buildings of 20+ (about 1,910 a year); their 2026 update estimates about 31% fewer, roughly 1,900 a year, and the size of the effect is still debated. Chicago voters turned down a version (Bring Chicago Home) in 2024, 53% to 47%.
Assumption: 18% fewer rezoned projects of 20+ homes get built (UCLA's first, smaller estimate), and 5% fewer of the homes Chicago builds anyway.

“Why not just build skyscrapers everywhere?”
Towers are the priciest homes to build, so they only work where rents are highest.

Steel-and-concrete high-rises cost about $65–71 more per square foot to build than shorter buildings (a Terner Center study of California projects), and they need elevators, deep foundations and extra fire safety. They pencil out downtown and next to the busiest stations, not on most blocks. Demand runs out too: even in 2021, forecast to be its best year since at least 1999, downtown Chicago was expected to fill about 6,500 more apartments. Loop zoning already allows supertalls; cost and financing are what stop them. That's why spreading mid-rises and 3–6-flats across the city adds more homes in the simulation than stacking towers in a few spots.

The 2-flats and 3-flats that define Chicago's neighborhoods are banned in much of the city today. 41% of Chicago is zoned for single-family homes or two-flats only (just 11% allows three-flats and up), and about a third of the single-family lots are smaller than the zoning code's minimum, so even a single house there needs special approval.
“New luxury buildings make rents go up.”
Usually the opposite: rents nearby tend to go down.

Higher-income renters who move into a new building would otherwise compete for older apartments nearby. A study of 11 US cities found rents near new buildings in lower-income areas ended up 5–7% lower than rents a bit farther away. In New York, adding 10% more homes within 500 feet lowered nearby rents about 1%.

“New homes only help rich people.”

When someone moves into a new apartment, they leave an older one empty, and the next person moves into that one. Researchers followed these chains of moves: every 100 new market-rate homes opened up the equivalent of 45–70 homes in below-median-income neighborhoods, mostly within a few years. Helsinki found about the same. It's slow, and it doesn't replace subsidies for the lowest incomes.

“Chicago's losing people. Why build more?”
Population barely moved, but the number of households grew.

Every household needs its own home, and more people live alone or in smaller households than they used to. So the same number of people needs more homes. From 2000 to 2020, Chicago added 80,761 households but only 48,162 homes, the only part of the region where homes fell behind households.
“More density means more crime and traffic.”
Not in Chicago's crime data, and each new neighbor drives a bit less.

A Chicago study found dense blocks mixing homes and shops have less crime than typical residential blocks, likely because more people are around to notice. On traffic, people in denser places drive slightly less each, not more: across many studies, 10% more density cuts driving per person about 0.4%. A block can still see more total trips, but homes near transit add fewer cars than the same homes at the edge of the region.

“Upzoning doesn't actually lower rents.”
Where cities did it at scale, rents grew slower or fell.

Minneapolis allowed more homes on more land: from 2017 to 2022 its rents rose 1% while the rest of Minnesota's rose 14%. Austin loosened its rules and built record numbers of homes, and median rent fell from $1,546 to $1,296 (2021–2026). Six years after Auckland, New Zealand upzoned about three-quarters of the city, 3-bedroom rents were an estimated 22–35% below where they'd been heading. It works slowly and alongside other factors, but the direction is consistent.

Chicago's Affordable Requirements Ordinance (ARO) makes many new buildings rent 10–20% of their units below market. Modeling for Los Angeles, where the affordable units serve households at 30% of median income, found total construction fell about 30% when the requirement rose from 11% to 25%, and affordable output topped out around 25%. Past that, both kinds of homes drop. Studies of real cities mostly find much smaller effects, from no clear drop to 5–8% fewer homes, so the exact tipping point is uncertain.
